## Passages
RESULT [agents]: Matches or exceeds subject-matter experts, who had full internet access, on three literature tasks. Its cited summaries are significantly more accurate than human-written Wikipedia articles. It finds 2.34 +/- 1.99 contradictions per biology paper, 70% of them validated by experts.
US [agents]: Shows that online research is a matter of scaffolding (retrieval, evidence gathering, citation checks) as much as raw model strength. A closed-loop agent can research online on its own if it is given a grounded retrieval tool and has to cite what it retrieves. This sweep did not verify how much weaker open-weight brains lose, so treat it as a hypothesis to measure on the cluster brains.
CORRECTION [agents]: Abstract confirms matching/exceeding experts without restricting their internet access on retrieval, summarization, contradiction detection; summaries more accurate than Wikipedia; 2.34 +/- 1.99 contradictions per paper, 70% validated.
RESULT [webresearch]: LitQA2: 85.2% ± 1.1% precision and 66.0% ± 1.2% accuracy, vs human experts' 73.8% precision and 67.7% accuracy. It finds 2.34 ± 1.99 contradictions per biology paper, 70% of them validated by experts. The paper's experiments used only frontier closed LLMs (GPT-4-Turbo orchestration), but the open-source paper-qa package supports Ollama, llama.cpp and LiteLLM, with Semantic Scholar/Crossref/Unpaywa [note truncated at collection]
US [webresearch]: Adopt the tool decomposition and the open-source package as the brain's literature tool. It can point at a local paper directory on the lab server and at our Ollama models. The README warns that local models must be 'relatively large' to follow its instructions, so it should run on a cluster brain, not the lab 3060 guide.
CORRECTION [webresearch]: Confirmed: LitQA2 precision 85.2% ± 1.1% and accuracy 66.0% ± 1.2%, against humans at 73.8% ± 9.6% precision and 67.7% ± 11.9% accuracy.
